entities.name: Simon of Kéza
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Simon of Kéza (c. 1250 – c. 1300) stands as the preeminent Hungarian chronicler of the late 13th century, a cleric and court historian whose singular work, the *Gesta Hungarorum* (Deeds of the Hungarians), profoundly shaped national identity for centuries. Serving as a priest in the royal court of King Ladislaus IV of Hungary, Kéza synthesized earlier Hungarian chronicles, oral traditions, and his own interpretations to construct a foundational narrative for the Hungarian nation. His chronicle is not merely a record of events but a deliberate ideological construct, legitimizing the Hungarian nobility and providing a mythical origin story for the Magyars, linking them to the Huns and Attila, thereby establishing a lineage of ancient power and prestige.

Kéza completed his *Gesta Hungarorum* around 1282–1285, likely during a period of political instability following the Mongol invasions and preceding the extinction of the Árpád dynasty. The work is divided into two main parts: the first details the origins and migrations of the Huns and Magyars, culminating in the conquest of the Carpathian Basin; the second provides a chronological history of Hungary up to Kéza's own time, concluding with the reign of Ladislaus IV. A distinctive feature is Kéza's theory of the "Scythian origin" of the Hungarians, asserting their descent from the Huns and, more broadly, from the ancient Scythians, a concept that imbued the Hungarian nobility with a sense of ancient, almost mythical, heritage and distinction from the common people.
